target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers and help low-income Americans vote.
objection: A federal holiday would not automatically give private-sector workers paid time off, so many low-income hourly employees in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and similar jobs would still be scheduled to work and would have to choose between voting and losing wages. That means the holiday could widen inequities rather than solve the schedule problem.

target: AG2's argument that low-income workers would still be disadvantaged because a holiday would leave private-employer scheduling untouched.
objection: The objection assumes a holiday can only be symbolic and cannot be paired with enforceable voting-time protections. Lawmakers could structure Election Day as a holiday with guaranteed time-to-vote requirements, potentially including pay protections or protected leave, which would remove the wage-versus-voting problem the objection depends on.

target: AG1's response that a federal holiday alone would reliably create usable non-working time for constrained workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave, so many essential service and customer-facing businesses can remain open and still schedule hourly employees. For those workers, the holiday may not translate into actual time off to vote, so the schedule barrier remains.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday does not reliably create usable non-working time.
objection: A holiday changes the baseline environment by closing schools and reducing overall demand, which often leads employers to shorten hours, reduce staffing, or close. That means more workers—including many hourly workers—actually do get usable time off, so the assumption that they will still be stuck working on election day is too strong.

target: AG1's contention that a holiday changes the baseline environment enough to create voting time for low-income workers.
objection: Even if schools and some employers shift their schedules, many private employers can remain open and keep hourly employees on shift. For those low-income workers, the holiday does not consistently become real non-working time, so the causal link from holiday to voting access is unreliable.

target: AG2's repeated assumption that low-income workers will still mostly be scheduled as usual under a holiday.
objection: A federal holiday changes more than a legal label: it shifts consumer activity and staffing patterns, so many employers reduce hours or close. As a result, many hourly workers are more likely to have usable non-working time than the objection suggests, undermining the claim that the holiday leaves them with essentially the same constraint.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday itself would move voting off the ordinary school/work calendar for constrained workers.
objection: Because federal holidays do not compel private employers to close or provide paid leave, workplaces in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar sectors can remain open and schedule shifts. So the holiday's effect on schedule barriers is uneven and depends on employer behavior that the policy does not mandate.

target: AG2's claim that holiday effects depend entirely on discretionary employer behavior and therefore won't reliably help low-income workers.
objection: That assumption overstates how unchanged private scheduling remains under a national holiday. A federally recognized holiday changes the operating baseline, often causing reduced staffing or closures in customer-facing industries and shifting school and transport calendars, which means a substantial portion of hourly workers will gain usable non-working time.

target: AG1's assertion that a holiday directly moves voting off the ordinary school/work calendar for the people most constrained by schedules.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or grant paid time off, so many low-income hourly workers can still be scheduled to work. In that case, the holiday does not reliably create real non-working time, and the choice between lost wages and voting persists.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is only a general nudge and has limited turnout impact compared with other reforms.
objection: The main barrier is that Election Day falls on a normal school/work day, which compresses usable hours for voting and forces many people to miss work or school. A national holiday directly changes those conditions by creating non-school, non-work time, so it is not merely a symbolic or indirect nudge.

target: AG1's argument that a national holiday changes default conditions enough to expand usable voting time.
objection: The hidden assumption is that constrained workers will actually have the day off or paid leave in practice. But private employers are not required to close or provide paid time off, so many low-income hourly workers may still have to work and face the same wage-versus-voting tradeoff.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is only a mild nudge and not a meaningful turnout reform.
objection: A holiday directly targets a major real-world turnout blocker: conflicts with school and work schedules. By changing schools' and many employers' operating conditions, it expands the number of voters with non-working time and is therefore more than a small convenience nudge.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would broadly raise turnout by giving most low-income hourly workers usable non-working time.
objection: That causal chain depends on the assumption that a federal holiday will actually give those workers time off without wage loss. Since private employers need not close or offer paid leave, many retail and service workers could still be scheduled, leaving the wage-versus-voting problem intact.

target: AG2's view that Election Day as a holiday is only a limited turnout-supporting reform.
objection: Election Day on a normal school/work day compresses the time available to vote and can force people to miss work or lose wages. A national holiday changes the default schedule and gives more people non-school, non-work time to vote, so it is a direct turnout-supporting reform rather than a minor convenience.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday shifts operating conditions enough to reduce work-schedule barriers for hourly workers.
objection: That relies on the weak assumption that a federal holiday will cause most low-income workers to get the day off or paid leave. Private employers are not required to do that, so many shift workers may still be scheduled and can face the same lost-wages-versus-voting choice.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday is just an indirect nudge with limited impact on turnout.
objection: A holiday directly changes the real-world schedule conditions that constrain voting by moving elections off an ordinary work/school day. That expands non-work, non-school time for voters and can meaningfully improve access, rather than merely nudging behavior.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday will broadly reduce time-budget pressure for the electorate.
objection: The causal link depends on assuming schools and many workplaces shifting hours is enough to create usable time for low-income hourly workers. But a federal holiday does not mandate private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many customer-facing workplaces can still schedule shifts and leave those workers with the same tradeoff between working and voting.

target: AG2's view that Election Day as a holiday is only a symbolic convenience and won't significantly improve turnout.
objection: Election Day currently falls on a normal school/work day, which compresses time for voting and often forces people to miss work or school. Making it a public holiday changes those default conditions and expands non-work time to vote, so the policy has a direct practical effect rather than just symbolic value.
